bridge: Builds on C05 machine execution, C06 memory and D09 evidence handling. The required native exercise uses a synthetic process snapshot; real malware execution is not required.
teaching:
Memory forensics observes a captured volatile state under a particular acquisition method. Tool compatibility depends on OS/build and image format. A parser failure or missing symbol data is not proof that a process is absent. Record the image provenance and compatible tool/version before interpreting output.

Reverse engineering infers program behaviour from code and artifacts. Static strings, imports and disassembly suggest capabilities, but may not establish that a path executed. Dynamic analysis adds observations under a particular environment and input; unfamiliar samples require specialist containment and should not be casually launched.

Triaging means prioritising evidence and uncertainty, not immediately naming a malware family. Compare process lineage, executable path, identity, memory mappings and network context. Legitimate software can exhibit suspicious-looking features. The synthetic exercise teaches corroboration without introducing a harmful binary.

Use an authorised training image and retain its hash, collection notes, operating-system identification, tool version and any symbol requirements. Memory analysis is an imperfect view captured during collection, not a complete historical recording. PIDs can be reused, parent processes may have exited and names can be misleading; corroborate process metadata with paths, command lines, signatures and other evidence. Recovered file content may be partial. Consult the current Volatility documentation for installation and exact plugin names. PowerShell cmdlet names are normally case-insensitive; the video’s capitalisation claim is incorrect. Never replace a reproducible tool version with an arbitrary development checkout just to match an old tutorial.
example:
Synthetic snapshot
PID10: editor, parent1, path /lab/editor, user A
PID11: helper, parent10, path /lab/helper, user A
PID12: helper, parent1, path /tmp/helper, user A
Connection: PID12 -> docs.example at09:05UTC
Unknown: binary hashes, command lines, content, execution history
Observation only: PID12 differs in path/lineage from PID11.
explanation: The same name helper does not prove the same binary or intent. A /tmp path may justify further review, but the packet does not establish malicious activity. A snapshot also lacks some history: a process that terminated earlier may not appear.
exercise: Build a triage table for all three PIDs with observed facts, alternative explanations and next evidence requested. State preservation requirements and why process names alone are weak identifiers.
solution: Request hashes, source/provenance, command lines, relevant logs and mapping details. Preserve the original snapshot/manifest. Do not call PID12 malware solely from its name, path or connection.
challenge: An analysis tool reports no PID12 on an image from an unsupported OS build. Explain the limitation and propose a validation step before claiming the process never existed.
challenge_solution: Unsupported parsing invalidates that absence claim. Verify tool/image compatibility and collection integrity, compare supported independent evidence and report the analysis gap. A different snapshot time can also explain differing process lists.
